abstract: Viruses of microbes inject their genome into host cells, take over host metabolism, and produce progeny virions that are released into the environment upon lysis. Environmental and host conditions shape viral traits, including the intracellular maturation rate of virions and the time between infection and lysis. The dependence of viral traits on environmental context, i.e., phenotypic plasticity, would appear to be inevitable for obligate intracellular parasites, which depend on host metabolic activity for replication. However, viruses, including viruses of microbes, encode genes that can decouple their replication from the host metabolic state. Here, we present a trait analysis and modeling framework to investigate how plasticity in maturation and lysis rates influences viral growth, invasion, and coexistence. First, analysis of experimental viral trait data shows support for high maturation rate plasticity and intermediate lysis rate plasticity across virus-microbe pairs. Next, leveraging an eco-evolutionary model, we find that viruses with high maturation rate plasticity outcompete other viruses when nutrient inflow is high or variable but not when nutrient inflow is low and stable. In addition, we find that high lysis rate plasticity maximizes viral invasion fitness and growth when nutrient density is high and susceptible cell density is low, or when environmental conditions are highly variable. These findings suggest that while plasticity is evolutionarily advantageous in a broad range of environments, decoupling viral traits (including both maturation and lysis rates) from host metabolism can be advantageous, even if costly, in environments with low resource inflow. Finally, we find that variation in plasticity can facilitate coexistence between viral types given a shared, susceptible host population. Overall, these results highlight the adaptive value of (de)coupling viral traits from environmental and host state and suggest new directions for exploring the link between plasticity and diversity for virus-microbe communities.
